q: Does the Google Cloud Generative AI Leader certification require technical experience?
a: No. It targets all roles and backgrounds; no technical experience required.

q: List the 5 courses of the Gen AI Leader path, in order.
a: 1 Beyond the Chatbot · 2 Unlock Foundational Concepts · 3 Navigate the Landscape · 4 Gen AI Apps: Transform Your Work · 5 Gen AI Agents: Transform Your Organization

q: Define generative AI (course wording, short).
a: A type of AI that creates new content and ideas — text, images, music, code.

q: Gemini vs the Gemini app — what is each?
a: Gemini = one of Google's gen AI models. The Gemini app = Google's gen AI chatbot application built on that model. Gen AI is a technology embedded into apps, not an app itself.

q: What are the 4 primary ways to use gen AI?
a: Create · Summarize · Discover · Automate

q: A bank uses gen AI anomaly detection to flag fraudulent transactions in real time. Which of the 4 uses?
a: Discover (monitoring real-time events / finding information at the right time).

q: A team converts content into accessible formats in real time with Text-to-Speech and Translation APIs. Which of the 4 uses?
a: Automate (automated format conversion).

q: Project managers auto-generate meeting notes with decisions and action items. Which use, and which tool?
a: Summarize — Gemini in Google Meet.

q: Which tool does the course cite for generating starter code for large software projects?
a: Gemini Code Assist.

q: Which tool does the course cite for automating contract review and information extraction?
a: Document AI.

q: Which tool does the course cite for creating video tutorials for customers?
a: Google Vids.

q: Which product gives employees agents combining Gemini reasoning, Google-quality search and enterprise data wherever it's hosted?
a: Gemini Enterprise.

q: Personalised streaming recommendations to reduce churn — which Google Cloud product does the course name?
a: Agent Search.

q: What is multimodal gen AI?
a: Gen AI that processes and integrates several formats (text, images, video, audio, PDFs) individually or combined at the same time.

q: Manufacturing safety: camera feeds + sensor data detect spills and alert workers. What capability is this an example of?
a: Multimodal gen AI (sensor data + video).

q: Key takeaway of 'business impact': businesses use Google Cloud gen AI for which 4 benefits?
a: Decision-making · efficiency & productivity · creative idea generation · cost reduction through automation.

q: What was Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform formerly called, and what is it?
a: Vertex AI. Google Cloud's unified ML platform to build, train and deploy ML models and AI apps.

q: Through which Agent Platform service do you access Google's large gen AI models across modalities?
a: Model Garden.

q: What is Agent Search (as described in the automotive use case)?
a: A fully managed, scalable Google Cloud service that lets developers add advanced search over large volumes of multimodal data to their apps.

q: Automotive virtual assistant: which product understood the driver, and which found the answer?
a: Gemini understood the questions; Agent Search retrieved the most relevant answer from manuals, FAQs, help articles, videos, guides.

q: 3 results of the automotive virtual assistant use case?
a: Reduced support costs · improved efficiency · enhanced accessibility.

q: One-liner: what is Agent Platform the key to?
a: Creating and deploying custom gen AI solutions for your business.

q: Define foundation models.
a: Large AI models trained on enormous, diverse datasets that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks.

q: Traditional AI model vs foundation model?
a: Traditional: single purpose, specific data (e.g. spam filter). Foundation: massive diverse data, adaptable to many tasks.

q: 3 key features of foundation models?
a: Trained on diverse data · flexible (one model, many use cases) · adaptable (specialise via targeted training).

q: True or false: all foundation models are LLMs.
a: False. All LLMs are foundation models; LLMs are the language-specialised type.

q: Chirp is trained on what, for what?
a: Multilingual audio — speech recognition (voice assistants, transcription, translation).

q: Nano Banana is trained primarily on what, for what?
a: Images + text descriptions; generates and edits images from text. Course name for Gemini's native image generation/editing. Exam guide names Imagen as the image model — learn both.

q: A decision tree that predicts customer churn — foundation model or not?
a: Not a foundation model (narrow, single-task).

q: Morrisons Product Finder: usage over Easter 2025?
a: ~50,000 hits per day.

q: Morrisons Product Finder: which 3 Google components and how did it work?
a: BigQuery (store product locations) + Vertex AI/Agent Platform + Gemini, which translates the shopper's query into product and location IDs.

q: Benefit of a pre-trained model cited by Morrisons regarding testing?
a: You don't exhaustively test the model itself — you test how it works in your environment.

q: What is a prompt?
a: The input given to a (foundation) model to produce an output.

q: 3 synonyms used for writing prompts?
a: Prompting, prompt engineering, prompt design.

q: Why are foundation models more flexible to prompt than many AI models?
a: Many models accept only one input type (numbers, emails, images); (multimodal) foundation models accept a much broader set of inputs.

q: You want a summary of troubleshooting steps from a support call. What input type do you give the model?
a: An audio file (the call recording) plus the request.

q: Google's mission statement (as quoted in the course)?
a: Organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful.

q: When did Google launch Google Cloud?
5 reasons to build on Google's gen AI ecosystem?
a: Individual productivity & efficiency · continuous improvement · responsible AI · enterprise ready · open approach.

q: What is SAIF?
a: Secure AI Framework — Google's tools and best practices for building secure AI systems.

q: Which Google offering provides threat intelligence to protect AI systems from cyberattacks?
a: Mandiant.

q: Compliance certifications cited as making Google Cloud 'enterprise ready'?
a: ISO 27001, SOC 2, HIPAA.

q: Examples of Google's 'open approach'?
a: Contributions to TensorFlow and PyTorch · open models and datasets · support for open standards.

q: Continuous improvement benefits of Google's ecosystem?
a: Automatic model upgrades · early access to new features · security patches and updates.

q: 3 elements of the most successful gen AI implementations?
a: Clear vision · focus on impactful use cases · tracking results.

q: Top-down vs bottom-up gen AI strategy?
a: Top-down: leadership sets a clear vision aligned to business priorities (priorities first, then AI). Bottom-up: teams closest to problems share challenges and experiment. Use both simultaneously.

q: Who is primarily responsible for securing funding and resources for gen AI?
a: Executives / high-level management.

q: Who is primarily responsible for identifying use cases in daily workflows and experimenting with tools?
a: Mid-level managers and individual contributors.

q: Who establishes ethical guidelines for responsible AI use?
a: Executives / high-level management.

q: 6 areas of the multi-directional gen AI strategy?
a: Strategic focus · exploration · responsible AI · resourcing · impact · continuous improvement.

q: Criteria for prioritising gen AI use cases (strategic focus)?
a: Feasible, actionable, affordable, high anticipated business value / ROI.

q: Where should initial gen AI exploration happen?
a: In low-risk areas of the business.

q: Which 3 enterprise tools support data governance in the strategy lesson, and what does each do?
a: Cloud Data Loss Prevention (discover/classify/de-identify data) · Cloud Key Management Service (encryption keys) · Google SecOps (detect/respond to threats).

q: Why does top-down matter even for bottom-up experiments?
a: It gives experiments a place in the overall strategy and keeps them safe and responsible.

q: What is the creative matrix?
a: A brainstorming method: axis 1 = gen AI options (product/modality), axis 2 = business items (personas/workflows/goals); sticky-note ideas at intersections, then rate impact vs effort.

q: After filling the creative matrix, what 2 dimensions do you evaluate ideas on?
a: Impact and feasibility (how much work to build).

q: Augmentation vs automation?
a: Augmentation: gen AI enhances human strategic work (critical thinking, creativity, relationships, planning). Automation: gen AI takes over repetitive/rule-based or time-consuming tasks.

q: A chatbot answers basic pricing/availability questions for sales. Augmentation or automation?
a: Automation.

q: An analyst uses gen AI reports to advise clients on investments. Augmentation or automation?
a: Augmentation.

q: 4 roles for humans-in-the-loop even in automation?
a: Data selection & preparation · prompt design & refinement · output evaluation & refinement · continuous monitoring & feedback.

q: Principle: shift human responsibility from ___ to ___.
a: From task execution to strategic thinking.

q: Warner Bros. Discovery Caption AI results?
a: ~50% reduction in overall costs; ~80% reduction in time to caption vs manual.

q: Caption AI workflow — what does the human do?
a: AI delivers a time-coded, formatted caption file; a human verifies words and sync (human-in-the-loop).

q: What platform property did WBD value in Vertex AI / Agent Platform?
a: It is model-agnostic — lets them pick the best model per use case beyond Google's own.

q: Two developments (around 2022) behind the gen AI explosion?
a: LLMs became far more capable · computing power for training/deploying became widely available.

q: Define AI, ML and gen AI in one line each.
a: AI: broad field of machines doing tasks needing human intelligence. ML: subset of AI where machines learn from data. Gen AI: application/subset that creates new content.

q: In this course, what is 'the model'?
a: The math (a system of equations with many parameters) built from data: input in, output out. Different data → different models.

q: Predictive (traditional) AI vs generative AI?
a: Predictive analyses data to predict/classify (spam or not). Generative learns patterns in data and creates new, similar content.

q: How do ML models make predictions (vs humans)?
a: They find patterns in data and calculate the likelihood (probability) of outcomes; humans use intuition.

q: 5 data-quality factors?
a: Accuracy · completeness · representativeness · consistency · relevance.

q: 3 data-accessibility factors?
a: Availability · cost · format.

q: A customer-preference dataset is missing a demographic, giving biased generalisations. Which quality factor failed?
a: Representativeness (representative/inclusive data).

q: Some records label sizes in cm, others in inches, confusing the model. Which quality factor failed?
a: Consistency.

q: A meteorologist predicts from just one day of data. Which quality factor failed?
a: Completeness (dataset size / sample).

q: Needed data exists but is behind paywalls or privacy restrictions. Which accessibility factor?
a: Availability.

q: London traffic data used to predict Kansas crop yields. Which quality factor failed?
a: Relevance.

q: Structured vs unstructured data?
a: Structured: predefined format, rows/columns, relational DBs (orders, bank statements, CSV). Unstructured: no predefined structure — text docs, emails, images, audio, video.

q: A medical record with date of birth, address, vaccination history fields — structured or unstructured?
a: Structured.

q: A free-text product review — structured or unstructured?
a: Unstructured.

q: What is the essential first step for any AI implementation (data lesson)?
a: Understanding your company's data — type, quality, availability, structure.

q: 3 primary ML approaches and their data?
a: Supervised (labeled data) · unsupervised (unlabeled data) · reinforcement (interaction + feedback/rewards).

q: Labeled vs unlabeled data?
a: Labeled: has tags (name/type/number) giving meaning. Unlabeled: raw, untagged.

q: Spam filter trained on emails tagged spam/not spam — which learning type?
a: Supervised.

q: Discovering customer segments from purchase history without predefined labels — which learning type?
a: Unsupervised.

q: A game AI learns by trial and error to maximise cumulative reward — which learning type?
a: Reinforcement.

q: Topic modelling on news articles — which learning type?
a: Unsupervised.

q: Fraud anomaly detection on transactions — which product and learning type (course example)?
a: BigQuery ML — unsupervised.

q: Predictive maintenance from machine sensor data — product and learning type?
a: Agent Platform — supervised.

q: Product recommendations continuously refined to maximise engagement — product and learning type?
a: Agent Platform — reinforcement learning.

q: 5 stages of the ML lifecycle?
a: Gather data (ingest) · prepare data · train model · deploy & predict · manage model.

q: Which Google Cloud tool handles real-time streaming data ingestion?
a: Pub/Sub.

q: Which tool is suited to storing unstructured data?
a: Cloud Storage.

q: Which tools manage structured data at ingestion?
a: Cloud SQL and Spanner.

q: Which tool does the course name for discovering datasets across the organisation (governance)? What is it called now?
a: Course: Data Catalog. Note: Data Catalog was discontinued on 1 June 2026, replaced by Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog). Not named in the exam guide.

q: Which tool is used in data prep to filter, fix inconsistencies and handle missing values?
a: BigQuery.

q: Which Agent Platform tool manages the features a model uses?
a: Agent Platform Feature Store.

q: Which Agent Platform tool automates ML tasks/workflows?
a: Agent Platform Pipelines.

q: Model management activities listed in the lifecycle?
a: Versioning · performance tracking · drift monitoring · feature management (Feature Store) · storing models · automation (Pipelines). Course says 'store models in Model Garden'; precise: Model Registry manages your model versions; Model Garden is for discovering and deploying available models.

q: What is drift monitoring?
a: Watching for changes in a model's accuracy/performance over time.

q: Which service ensures only the right people access data across the lifecycle?
a: Identity and Access Management (IAM).

q: What is deep learning?
a: A subset of ML using (multi-layer) artificial neural networks to process complex patterns.

q: What is semi-supervised learning?
a: Training on a small amount of labeled data plus a large amount of unlabeled data.

q: What are diffusion models?
a: Foundation models that generate high-quality images, audio, video by iteratively refining noise into structured data.

q: Summary: DL, foundation models, gen AI relationship?
a: Deep learning = core technology; foundation models = architectures built on DL; gen AI = applying them to create new content.

q: Define ML as in the definitions quiz.
a: A subset of AI that lets machines learn from data without explicit programming, improving over time.

q: 8 factors when choosing a gen AI model?
a: Modality · context window · security · availability & reliability · cost · performance · fine-tuning & customisation · ease of integration.

q: What is the context window, and its trade-off?
a: How much information the model considers at once. Larger = more coherent on long tasks but higher compute cost.

q: Key cost principle when choosing models?
a: Match the model to the task — bigger isn't always better, multimodal isn't always needed.

q: Gemini vs Gemma?
a: Gemini: multimodal model (text, images, audio, video). Gemma: family of lightweight, open models built from Gemini research, for local/specialised deployments.

q: Imagen vs Veo (exam guide's named models)?
a: Imagen: text-to-image diffusion model (high-quality images from text, editing). Veo: video generation from text or images. The course also mentions Nano Banana for images; the exam guide names Imagen.

q: Which model sources can you access via Agent Platform?
a: Google models — exam guide lists Gemini, Gemma, Imagen, Veo (course also shows Nano Banana) — plus proprietary third-party models and openly available models.

q: Availability & reliability factors to check?
a: Uptime guarantees, redundancy, disaster recovery.

q: You need to generate image captions (image in, text out). Which model property is mandatory?
a: Multimodality.

q: Define grounding.
a: Connecting/tying a model's output to specific, verifiable sources of information (e.g. company data) to improve accuracy and relevance.

q: 6 foundation model limitations?
a: Data dependency · knowledge cutoff · bias · fairness · hallucinations · edge cases.

q: What is a knowledge cutoff?
a: The last date the model was trained on new information; it doesn't know later events.

q: What is a hallucination?
a: Output that isn't accurate or based on real information — models can't verify against external sources, so answers can sound convincing yet be wrong.

q: Bias vs fairness limitation?
a: Bias: unbalanced training data that models can amplify. Fairness: even with balanced data, defining fairness is complex and assessments only cover specific bias categories.

q: What are edge cases?
a: Rare, atypical scenarios that expose model weaknesses (errors, unexpected results).

q: 3 benefits of grounding?
a: Reduces hallucinations · anchors responses in your data · builds trust (citations, confidence scores).

q: 3 phases of RAG?
a: Retrieval → augmentation (add to prompt) → generation.

q: What kind of index does RAG retrieval use?
a: One that understands semantic meaning, not just keywords.

q: Relationship between grounding, RAG and fine-tuning?
a: Course framing: grounding is the goal, RAG is a technique to achieve it, fine-tuning 'improves grounding in a domain'. Precise: grounding anchors answers to verifiable sources when the model answers; fine-tuning changes the model's parameters/behaviour and does not by itself cite sources or add fresh facts.

q: Main limitation of prompt engineering?
a: Limited to the model's existing knowledge — it can't produce what the model never learned.

q: What is fine-tuning and when is it used?
a: Further training a pre-trained model on a task-specific dataset (adjusting parameters). Used when prompting isn't enough, for specific tasks/output formats, especially with examples of desired output.

q: You need answers based on today's internal policy documents. Prompting, fine-tuning or RAG?
a: RAG (grounding in up-to-date external knowledge).

q: You need a model to always output in a specific style/format and you have many examples. Best technique?
a: Fine-tuning.

q: Fastest, simplest way to give a model supplementary context?
a: Prompt engineering.

q: 5 areas where humans-in-the-loop are key?
a: Content moderation · sensitive applications (healthcare, finance) · high-risk decisions · pre-generation review · post-generation review.

q: Pre-generation vs post-generation review?
a: Pre: experts validate outputs before deployment. Post: continuous review after deployment to adapt and improve.

q: Fine-tuning process steps?
a: Select pre-trained model → gather data → train → evaluate & refine.

q: Define Secure AI.
a: Preventing intentional harm: protecting AI systems from malicious attacks and misuse across the full lifecycle.

q: What is data poisoning?
a: Attackers corrupt training data with manipulated data so the model learns wrong patterns and makes flawed predictions.

q: AI security risks named in the Secure AI takeaway?
a: Data poisoning · model theft · prompt injection.

q: What does SAIF help organisations do?
a: Find and stop threats · automatically strengthen defences · manage each AI system's unique risks; integrates with existing security so models are secure by default.

q: Which tool gives a centralised view of security posture across Google Cloud?
a: Security Command Center.

q: Who shares threat research to identify and disrupt malicious activity?
a: Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant (plus Mandiant Consulting for guidance).

q: How does Google Cloud protect data at the infrastructure level?
a: Secure-by-design infrastructure; encryption in transit and at rest; IAM for granular access.

q: Secure AI vs Responsible AI?
a: Secure AI: intentional harm (attacks). Responsible AI: avoiding intentional AND unintentional harm. Security is the foundation of responsible AI.

q: Responsible AI themes covered?
a: Security foundation · transparency · privacy · data quality, bias & fairness · accountability & explainability · legal implications.

q: How is privacy protected in training data?
a: Anonymising or pseudonymising data; safeguards against models leaking sensitive training data.

q: Purpose of explainable AI?
a: Make AI decision-making transparent and understandable — trust, debugging, uncovering hidden bias.

q: Which Google Cloud tool helps understand model outputs and identify bias?
a: Vertex Explainable AI.

q: Key legal areas in AI development?
a: Data privacy · non-discrimination · intellectual property · product liability.

q: A resume-screening tool favours one demographic because of historical hiring data. What issue?
a: Bias inherited from training data → fairness problem.

q: How can AI perpetuate societal biases?
a: Through biased training data, biased developers, or biased deployment environments.

q: Fairness requires what?
a: Accountability — knowing who is responsible and how the AI decides (explainability).

q: 3 questions Course 3 answers?
a: What are the layers of building gen AI · what Google Cloud options exist · when to choose one solution over another.

q: 5 layers of the gen AI landscape (bottom → top)?
a: Infrastructure · models · platform · agents · gen AI powered applications.

q: Agent layer definition (layers lesson)?
a: Software that works out how best to achieve a goal using its inputs and available tools: autonomous action and multi-step tasks a model alone can't do. Course says agents 'independently set goals'; in practice they pursue a goal they are given.

q: What does the platform layer provide?
a: APIs, data management, model deployment tools — the backbone bridging models and agents and hiding infrastructure complexity.

q: What does the infrastructure layer include?
a: Core compute: physical hardware (servers, GPUs, TPUs) and software to store and run models and data.

q: Engine analogy: what is each layer?
a: Infrastructure = foundation · models = core · platform = connects everything · agents = drivers · applications = vehicles.

q: Which layer is the 'brain' of the agent?
a: The model layer.

q: Definition of a gen AI agent (memorise).
a: An application that tries to achieve a goal by observing the world and acting upon it using the tools at its disposal.

q: 3 capabilities agents bring to applications?
a: Understanding/responding to natural language · automating complex multi-step tasks · personalisation.

q: What is a multi-agent system?
a: Several specialised agents working together within one application.

q: Which Google Cloud tool lets teams create agents in natural language instead of complex code?
a: AI Applications.

q: Agents vs applications — roles?
a: Agents add intelligence and automation; applications provide the UI, framework, goals and purpose.

q: Conversational vs workflow agents?
a: Conversational: understand intent and dialogue with users. Workflow: automate tasks/multi-step processes triggered by events.

q: 5 steps of a conversational agent?
a: You provide input → agent understands intent → calls a tool if needed → generates a response → delivers it.

q: An agent processes orders, updates inventory, sends shipping notices and handles returns. Which type?
a: Workflow agent.

q: An agent inspects security logs, flags anomalies, opens a ticket and assigns humans. Which type and family?
a: Workflow agent; security agent use case.

q: Which Gemini feature is cited for autonomous in-depth research reports?
a: Gemini Deep Research.

q: 6 agent use-case families?
a: Customer service · employee productivity · creative · code · data · security.

q: 2 elements that distinguish agents from standalone models?
a: A reasoning loop and tools.

q: 4 steps of the reasoning loop?
a: Observe · interpret · plan · act (repeat until goal or stopping point).

q: What are tools for an agent?
a: Functionalities letting the agent interact with its environment — data, software apps, even physical robots.

q: 2 prompt-engineering frameworks named for reasoning loops?
a: ReAct and chain-of-thought (CoT).

q: Writing assistant: generating grammatical, stylistic text — model or agent function?
a: Model.

q: Learning platform: tracking progress and adapting the learning plan — model or agent function?
a: Agent.

q: 6 key features of Agent Platform?
a: Open & flexible (no lock-in) · powerful infrastructure · pre-trained models · comprehensive tooling · customisation (built-in IDE) · easy integration (APIs).

q: What is MLOps?
a: Practices/tools that automate, standardise and manage the ML project lifecycle for collaboration and continuous improvement.

q: Training capabilities Agent Platform manages for you?
a: Fully managed compute · ML-optimised training jobs · distributed training · hyperparameter optimisation · enterprise security.

q: You need to track experiments, manage model versions and keep a change record. Which tool?
a: Model Registry.

q: A deployed model's performance is declining (drift/skew). Which tool detects it and triggers retraining?
a: Model Monitoring.

q: Automate the ML pipeline from preprocessing to deployment. Which tool?
a: Agent Platform Pipelines.

q: Compare candidate models' performance to pick the best. Which tool?
a: Model Evaluation.

q: Share, serve and reuse ML features consistently across teams. Which tool?
a: Agent Platform Feature Store.

q: What does Model Garden offer (course figure on size)?
a: Discover, customise and deploy models from Google, partners and open source. Course said 'over 160 models'; the figure keeps changing — don't memorise the number.

q: What does Model Garden let you do?
a: Discover, customise and deploy existing models from Google and partners (Google, third-party, open-source).

q: 4 model categories in Model Garden?
a: First-party foundation models · first-party pre-trained APIs · open models · third-party models.

q: Which model in Model Garden is for text-to-image? Text/image-to-video? Speech-to-text?

q: Examples of open models in Model Garden?

q: First-party pre-trained APIs listed?

q: Custom training vs AutoML on Agent Platform?
a: Custom: any framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, XGBoost), full control. AutoML: train models with minimal technical knowledge and effort.

q: AutoML objectives per data type?
a: Image: classification, object detection. Video: action recognition, classification, object tracking. Tabular: classification/regression, forecasting.

q: Translation for a global e-commerce site, fast, moderate budget. Build custom or Model Garden?
a: Model Garden (existing model / pre-trained API).

q: Researcher needs complete control of architecture and training for protein folding. Option?
a: Build a custom model on Agent Platform.

q: Cymbal Aerospace: two-layered solution for CAD files?

q: Cymbal Aerospace results?
a: Product development cycles 15% faster · design review time -20% · manufacturing planning bottlenecks eliminated.

q: How did Cymbal Aerospace deploy without managing servers?
a: Serverless infrastructure; Agent Platform handled MLOps (scaling, infrastructure).

q: Infrastructure layer = ?
a: Hardware + software providing compute, storage and networking to train, deploy and scale models.

q: GPU vs TPU?
a: GPU: originally for graphics, general-purpose parallel processing. TPU: Google's custom chip optimised specifically for AI.

q: What is a hypercomputer?
a: A supercomputer made by linking many nodes (with GPUs/TPUs) over high-speed networks to act as one unit.

q: What does throughput mean in storage?
a: The amount of work done within a specific period of time.

q: 3 benefits of Google Cloud infrastructure for teams?
a: Scalability · performance · cost-effectiveness.

q: What network property does Google's global fiber network provide?
a: High bandwidth, low latency.

q: Define edge computing.
a: Running AI on devices or servers closer to the data source or point of need.

q: Benefits of edge AI?
a: Real-time responsiveness · data privacy · less reliance on internet connectivity (offline).

q: What is LiteRT?
a: Lite Runtime — Google's high-performance runtime to run ML models efficiently on-device.

q: What is Gemini Nano and where is it used?
a: Google's most efficient, compact Gemini model for on-device use. Pixel (Call Notes, Recorder summaries) and Android via AI Edge SDK.

q: Agent Platform steps to deploy to edge?

q: Medical device giving real-time feedback during surgery — edge or cloud?
a: Edge (latency).

q: Chatbot handling millions of e-commerce queries daily — edge or cloud?
a: Cloud (scale).

q: Smart-city traffic optimisation analysis — edge or cloud?
a: Cloud (centralised capacity).

q: Business leaders vs developers vs AI practitioners — typical tools?
a: Leaders: pre-built solutions (Workspace with Gemini). Developers: AI Applications, pre-trained APIs, Agent Platform to build agents. AI practitioners: customise/deploy/optimise models on Agent Platform, BigQuery integration, bias detection, adversarial testing.

q: 3 activities you pay for in gen AI?

q: What is a token?
a: A piece of text — a word or part of a word.

q: 4 main needs to assess before a gen AI project?
a: Scale · customisation · user interaction · privacy.

q: 4 'other considerations' in solution needs?
a: Latency · connectivity · accuracy · explainability.

q: Individual or small team needs — which approach?
a: Leverage pre-built tools / existing gen AI apps.

q: Specialised domain (law, medicine) — customisation advice?
a: Course: fine-tune with domain-specific data or use domain-trained models. Exam rule of thumb: fresh or proprietary FACTS → RAG/grounding; domain STYLE, format or behaviour → fine-tuning.

q: Marketing images from text, some coding skills, short on time. Best path?
a: Use a pre-trained API.

q: Regulations named for compliance?
a: GDPR, HIPAA.

q: Where is explainability especially crucial?
a: Healthcare and finance.

q: 4 steps to compare providers/models?
a: Evaluate capabilities (benchmarks) · compare pricing vs expected usage · factor in extra costs (storage, API calls, fine-tuning) · read the fine print.

q: Resources for comparing models?

q: 5 maintenance areas to plan?
a: Model monitoring & retraining · data updates · software updates & bug fixes · hardware & infrastructure · security & compliance.

q: Why use Google Cloud's fully managed environment for maintenance?
a: Developers focus on agent development, not infrastructure; the platform handles deployment and model improvement, maximising ROI.

q: Deterministic vs generative agents?
a: Deterministic: predefined paths, workflow/event-driven, same input → same output, high control. Generative: LLM-based intent understanding, more flexible, some randomness.

q: Order of agent evolution (oldest → newest)?
a: Deterministic → generative without RAG → generative with RAG → today: hybrid.

q: Which components did deterministic agents have?

q: What are sampling parameters?
a: Settings ('knobs') sent with a prompt that influence model behaviour/output.

q: Token rule of thumb in English?
a: 1 token ≈ 4 characters; 100 tokens ≈ 60–80 words.

q: What does temperature control?
a: Randomness/creativity. Low = focused, deterministic, repeatable. High = diverse, unpredictable.

q: What is top-p (nucleus sampling)?
a: Sample from the smallest set of most-likely tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p. Lower = focused; higher = diverse.

q: What is top-k?
a: Sample randomly from the k most likely tokens.

q: Why prefer top-p over top-k?
a: Top-p's candidate set size adapts dynamically to the probability distribution; a fixed k can give strange results when the distribution is skewed.

q: You need concise, factual answers (Q&A/summaries). How to set parameters?
a: Low temperature and shorter output length (lower top-p).

q: You need creative, open-ended text. How to set parameters?
a: Raise temperature and top-p.

q: What is natural language processing (NLP)?
a: The branch of AI that lets computers understand, interpret and generate human language (text and speech). LLMs are a modern, foundation-model approach to NLP.

q: Prompt tuning vs prompt engineering?
a: Prompt engineering: writing better text instructions; the model is unchanged. Prompt tuning: a lightweight tuning method that learns a small set of extra 'soft prompt' parameters added to the input while the base model's weights stay frozen — cheaper than full fine-tuning.

q: Fine-tuning vs grounding — what does each actually change?
a: Fine-tuning changes the model itself (parameters) to shift style, format or task behaviour. Grounding leaves the model as is and connects each answer to verifiable sources at answer time (e.g. RAG, Google Search).

q: A bank wants answers based on this week's internal policy updates, with citations. Fine-tuning or RAG?

q: Model Garden vs Model Registry?

q: Security measure per ML lifecycle stage (Secure AI lesson)?
a: Gather data: access controls on who reads/adds data (stops data poisoning) · Prepare: anonymise sensitive data, validate integrity, anomaly detection, encrypt, log/monitor · Train: protect training data and model parameters (model theft) · Deploy: control who can use the model, verify pre-built model sources · Manage: monitor for tampering/anomalies, patch, review access.

q: What is the key security concern in the model TRAINING phase?
a: Protecting training data and model parameters from unauthorised access or modification — including model theft.

q: What is an adversarial attack, and what defends against it?
a: Feeding the model misleading inputs to trick it. Defend by filtering, sanitising and checking inputs, and monitoring outputs to stop leaks or harmful content.

q: Google Cloud security tools named in the exam guide?

q: Anonymization vs pseudonymization?
a: Anonymization removes identifying details so data can't be linked back to a person. Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with substitutes (tokens) that can be re-linked only with separately protected information.

q: Privacy risks to consider in gen AI?
a: Personal data in training data · models leaking sensitive training data in outputs · re-identification · using data without consent.
